title: Inequities and determinants of cesarean section delivery in Malawi: A multilevel analysis of 2024 demographic and health survey
content:
by Habtu Kifle Negash

Background

Cesarean section (CS) is a life-saving surgical procedure for childbirth complications, but its use varies widely. Globally, CS rates have risen from 7% in 1990 to 21% in recent years, with disparities between high- and low-income countries. Sub-Saharan Africa, including Malawi, has some of the lowest CS coverage, despite high institutional delivery rates. Its use is influenced by individual and community factors, reflecting inequities in obstetric care. This study assessed the prevalence and determinants of CS among reproductive-age women in Malawi.

Methods

A cross-sectional study was conducted using secondary data from the 2024 Malawi Demographic and Health Survey, including a weighted sample of 6,798 women aged 15–49 years. Descriptive statistics summarized participant characteristics and CS prevalence. Multilevel logistic regression was employed to identify individual- and community-level determinants, accounting for clustering effects. Adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05.

Results

The overall prevalence of cesarean section was 11.32% (n = 769.72; 95% CI: 10.59–12.10%), with regional variation: Northern 13.03%, Central 12.67%, and Southern 9.70%. Factors positively associated with CS included maternal age 25–34 (AOR = 1.35; 95% CI: 1.06–1.71) and 35–49 years (AOR = 1.82; 95% CI: 1.27–2.63), higher education (secondary or above: AOR = 1.91; 95% CI: 1.22–2.99), richest household wealth (AOR = 1.57; 95% CI: 1.13–2.18), first birth at age ≥ 20 years (AOR = 1.26; 95% CI: 1.05–1.52), male child (AOR = 1.31; 95% CI: 1.12–1.54), high/unknown birth weight, and multiple pregnancies (AOR = 4.56; 95% CI: 2.87–7.26). Multiparity and rural residence were associated with lower odds of CS.

Conclusions

Cesarean section utilization in Malawi is unevenly distributed across regions. Both individual- and community-level factors influence CS delivery. Targeted interventions addressing maternal education, socioeconomic disparities, and rural healthcare access are recommended to improve equitable access to cesarean services.
